ideas.title: Sled the cart down the dune: plough to brake, lean to steer, tip if you lean wrong
ideas.nearest: A snowball that grows as it rolls, a take that misses
ideas.critique: Round 1's sled is now one passive-pressure model for every blade in sand, with steering and rollover coming from per-wheel loads instead of a turn rate, which answers 'the brake has to feel real'. It is also the only pitch with the player steering live and friends reacting on screen. The risk is scope: if it ends up as McKyes with one cohesion and one friction angle typed in, plus a load transfer tuned so the cart tips on cue, it is a one-dune rig, and the shrieking ponies will be judged as animation, not as canned cheers.

ideas.title: Form the first lead cell: the plates change colour as they learn to hold charge
ideas.critique: It answers round 1's objection by making the forming itself the shot: per-patch Butler-Volmer, Faraday growth and shedding, with brown spreading and a thin-film tint, is real electrochemistry shown as a material, which is Hikari's strength. Still, it is a jar by the workbench filmed through glass while a current runs, the island's most worn form, and a once-a-day crank where you watch a colour creep is a slow loop to play.

ideas.title: Work any metal cold: one plasticity for lead, copper and iron
ideas.nearest: A copper wire keeps its bends
ideas.critique: Generalising round 1's lead-only rig into J2 plasticity with each metal's own yield, hardening and recrystallisation answers the one-material worry, and being able to feel copper stiffen until you anneal it is real material behaviour in your hands. What is predictable is the payoff: a sheet that comes out flatter than it went in, filmed close on a rock, with 'learning where to hit' as a thin skill unless the uneven thickness truly decides how the parts work later.
